t: Before the 4th century BCE Macedon was a small kingdom centred on Aigai, briefly a vassal of the Achaemenid Empire under Amyntas I and Alexander I, who fought on the Persian side at Plataea in 479 BCE.
Philip II (359–336 BCE) rebuilt the army around the sarissa-armed phalanx, took the mines of Crenides and Amphipolis, and defeated Athens and Thebes at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE.
Elected hegemon of the League of Corinth in 337 BCE, Philip was assassinated by his bodyguard Pausanias of Orestis at his daughter's wedding feast at Aigai in 336 BCE, and Alexander succeeded him.
dyk: Alexander I of Macedon was at first refused entry to the foot race at the Olympic Games because only Greeks could compete; he produced an Argead genealogy tracing his line to Temenus of Argos, and the Hellanodikai let him run.
ev: One of the earliest Argead kings establishes Aigai as the capital, in Robert Malcolm Errington's reckoning.
Amyntas I reigns, the first king of whom much is known; the Persian general Megabazus persuades him to submit as a vassal of the Achaemenid Empire.
Macedonian soldiers fight on the Persian side at the Battle of Plataea; the Achaemenid withdrawal from Europe soon ends Persian control of Macedonia.
Archelaus I moves the capital north to Pella, improves the coinage and brings Euripides to his court; his assassination plunges the kingdom into chaos.
Bardylis's Illyrians kill Perdiccas III and 4,000 Macedonian troops in battle; Philip II accedes at twenty-four.
Philip II defeats Onomarchus at the Battle of Crocus Field and is elected archon of the Thessalian League.
Philip II defeats Athens and Thebes at the Battle of Chaeronea and forms the League of Corinth, which elects him hegemon in 337 BCE.
Philip II is assassinated by Pausanias of Orestis at Aigai; the army and leading aristocrats proclaim Alexander III king.

f.capital: Aigai (modern Vergina), from the mid-7th century BCE; Pella from the reign of Archelaus I (413–399 BCE), Aigai remaining the ceremonial and religious centre
f.founder: Perdiccas I or Caranus, by contradictory legends; the dynasty claimed descent from Temenus of Argos and Heracles
f.predecessor: The small tribal kingdoms of Lower and Upper Macedonia, each under its own petty king
f.successor: The Macedonian Empire of Alexander the Great (336–323 BCE), then the Antipatrid and Antigonid kingdoms of Macedon
